description:
We’re The Royal Beauties, a team of curious minds who believe space belongs to everyone. We joined this hackathon to take on real challenges with NASA’s open data and build tools that are useful, beautiful and easy for anyone to use.

Between us we cover coding, design, science and storytelling. We like problems that mix data with imagination, like reading what satellites see, mapping how our planet changes, and making science easier to understand.
summary:
Earth Jukebox with Agent Julie is a browser game for children aged 7 to 10. It turns real NASA pictures of Earth at night into music. Kids pick a picture, such as India, Europe, the Nile or the whole world, and every city light becomes a note they can see, hear and play.

Main concept: pictures and data can be heard, not only seen. Along the way kids learn five music ideas:

Melody: higher lights play higher notes.
Harmony: lights in the same column sing a chord together.
Tempo: more light makes faster music.
Rhythm: busy areas get shorter notes.
Timbre: each colour plays a different instrument.

In the Earth Time Machine, kids hear the night lights year by year from 2012 to 2023. They can hear India’s lights more than double, which shows them that Earth is changing. Missions, quizzes and patches keep it playful.

Agent Julie’s inspiration: she is an original cartoon astronaut named in honour of Canadian astronaut Julie Payette, and she isn’t meant to look like her. Payette flew to the International Space Station, which ties in with the game’s photo taken from the station. Julie’s French greetings, like “Bonjour!” and “Allons-y!”, may also nod to Payette’s Québec roots, but the project files don’t say so directly.
details:
How pictures become music

  1. Find the lights. Each pixel's brightness is compared with its neighbourhood (local contrast), so cities stand out while large grey areas such as ice stay quiet. Touching bright pixels are grouped into clusters and ranked by total brightness. The brightest ones (up to 150) become the "stars" a child can tap.
  2. Turn data into music.

What the picture shows

What you hear

Music idea

Height of a light

Pitch: higher light, higher note (48 white-key notes)

Melody

Lights in the same column

Notes played together, snapped to the C, F, G or Am chord

Harmony

Total light in a frame

Speed of the music and extra instrument layers

Tempo

Number of lights in a slice of the picture

Note length, from quarter notes down to sixteenth notes

Rhythm

Colour of a light

Instrument

Timbre

Brightness and size of a light

Volume and sparkle

  1. Measure change. The app measures the total night light in each year's EIC frame. Compared with 2012: World +64%, India +125%, the Nile region +28%, and Western Europe about the same (−7%). In the Earth Time Machine children hear this growth as more notes, a faster tempo and more instruments.

The experience the team designed

  • Agent Julie, an original cartoon astronaut and "music detective" named in honour of Canadian astronaut Julie Payette, guides the child with short messages she can read aloud.
  • Five music missions: Earth Time Machine (tempo, melody, harmony), Star Melody (melody), Star Choir (harmony), Rocket Tempo (tempo) and Music Sandbox (melody, harmony, rhythm).
  • Learning tools: a music-word explainer with a "Show me on the picture!" demo, an instrument picker, a "lights" slider from brightest-only to dim lights, and a 3-question quiz per mission that earns a medal.

Development process

  1. Concept and design (team): we chose the EIC night lights, defined the audience and learning goals, designed the missions and Agent Julie, and decided how each part of a picture should map to a music idea.
  2. Building the prototype (team + AI): the team described the design, and AI (Claude) wrote the code for the light detection, the sound engine, the missions, the quizzes and Agent Julie. The team played every version, reviewed it and asked for changes.
  3. Guide website: a companion site explains the challenge, the idea, the picture-to-music mapping, how to play each mission, the measured results and notes for teachers.
  4. Polish: mobile and touch support, short gameplay videos and a captioned 30-second intro video, and a "📖 How to play" link from the game to the guide.
  5. Transparency: an SI disclosure file, header comments and metadata tags in the code, and a visible "SI-generated" watermark on every screenshot, video and on the Agent Julie drawing. Nothing uses NASA logos, flags or mission patches.
